title: Sikhism: the free kitchen
hook: in every gurdwara, anyone may eat, sitting together on the floor as equals

segments.voice: Yesterday: vand chhakna, sharing what you earn. Your line was share it. Did something of yours end up on someone else's plate? Day two hundred seventy-eight.

A long hall, a clean floor, long strips of cloth laid down in rows. A student sits down. Next to her, a taxi driver still in his work jacket. Then a grandmother, a tourist with a backpack, a man who hasn't eaten since yesterday. Volunteers walk down the rows with buckets and ladles: lentils, a vegetable curry, warm flatbread dropped into open hands. Nobody asks your name, your religion or whether you can pay. Nobody gets a better seat. Today, on our visit to Sikhism: the free kitchen, and the idea of sitting together.
screen: `A LONG HALL, ROWS ON THE FLOOR.` → `NO NAMES, NO BILL, NO BETTER SEAT.` → `THE FREE KITCHEN.`

segments.voice: The word is langar. It means the community kitchen that belongs to every gurdwara, the Sikh house of worship, and also the meal served there. Sikh tradition traces it to Guru Nanak, the first Guru. It grew under the second Guru, Guru Angad, and Sikhs especially remember his wife, Mata Khivi, who ran the kitchen and made sure the food was generous. Sikh tradition remembers why it mattered. In that world, who could eat with whom was bound up with caste, and eating side by side crossed lines people had been raised not to cross. The third Guru, Guru Amar Das, made it a rule, remembered in a short Punjabi phrase: pehle pangat, piche sangat. First sit in the row, then join the gathering. A story Sikhs tell says that even the Mughal emperor Akbar, coming to see the Guru, first sat on the floor and ate in the row like everyone else. The historical details of that visit are debated, but the point of the story isn't. The food is simple and vegetarian, so that people of almost any diet or faith can eat it. It's cooked and served by volunteers, as seva, selfless service. And it runs at every scale, from a small gurdwara's kitchen to the vast langar at the Golden Temple in Amritsar, where still nobody pays. So langar is two lessons at once. Yesterday's: share what you have. And today's: when you share, sit at the same level. Nobody above, nobody below. Everyone sits together.
screen: `LANGAR — THE COMMUNITY KITCHEN.` · `GURU NANAK, GURU ANGAD, MATA KHIVI.` · `FIRST SIT IN THE ROW.` · `SIMPLE FOOD, SERVED AS SEVA.` · then, large: `EVERYONE SITS TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: For the sit, picture a row on a floor. Put yourself in it. Now fill the places beside you: someone you love, someone you pass every day and never speak to, someone you find hard. Everyone at the same height, the same plate. Just notice how that feels, where it's easy and where it pinches. The bell holds the time.
Langar. The free community kitchen of the gurdwara, and the meal shared there, where everyone eats at the same level. Today's word.
Your line: everyone sits together. Today, eat one meal or one coffee with someone different from you, a coworker you don't know, a neighbor, someone older or younger. Day two hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Gurdwaras keep a langar where volunteers cook and serve a free vegetarian meal to anyone who comes, traditionally seated together in rows on the floor.

notes: Review 2026-10-01: hook no longer opens 'Picture'; cut the 'early fifteen hundreds' date and the 'tens of thousands a day' figure; caste context framed as Sikh tradition's memory; howItsDone drops 'every'.
Mata Khivi's role in the langar is praised in the vaar of Balvand and Satta (Ang 967); confirm the Ang reference.
'Pehle pangat, piche sangat' attributed to Guru Amar Das: confirm the phrasing and transliteration.
Akbar eating in the langar is told as a story Sikhs tell; details of the meeting are debated by historians.
Golden Temple langar 'tens of thousands a day': commonly reported figures run 50,000 to 100,000; kept deliberately general.
Some gurdwaras outside India have used tables and chairs, and this has been debated; the script says 'traditionally' on the floor in howItsDone.
